\chapter{The German Weekend}
\label{ch:ge-wochenende}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name both German words for Saturday and the word for Sunday, and say which of them German inherited and which it bought.}

The weekend is where the weekday pattern breaks a second time. Samstag is not Saturn's day but the Sabbath — Hebrew shabbāt by way of Greek — while Sonntag is the sun's, a day the Church renamed in Romance and left alone here. It closes on Sonnabend, the northern Saturday, which is transparent the moment Sonne and Abend are both owned.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[die Sonne]{die Sonne — \textquotedblleft{}the sun\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C07-sonne}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{der Mond}. Its opposite number comes with a surprise attached, and the surprise is the article.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: die Sonne}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{die Sonne} — \textquotedblleft{}the sun.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Same word as English \textbf{sun}, with the German ending. But notice the pair you now own: \emph{\textbf{der}} \emph{Mond} and \emph{\textbf{die}} \emph{Sonne}. The moon is masculine and the sun is feminine.

\begin{culture}
That is the \textbf{reverse} of what the Romance languages do, where the sun is masculine and the moon feminine — French \emph{le soleil} and \emph{la lune}, Spanish \emph{el sol} and \emph{la luna}.

Neither is a statement about the sun. Grammatical gender is a filing system, not a description, and the two families filed the same two objects in opposite drawers. It is worth meeting early, because it is the clearest possible proof that a German noun's gender is not something you can reason out from the thing itself.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die Sonne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair with their articles — \textquotedblleft{}der Mond, die Sonne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the other way round — \textquotedblleft{}le soleil, la lune\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Mond, die Sonne.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the sun.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Die Sonne}.) Which article does the moon take? (\emph{\textbf{Der}}.) Which way round is French? (\textbf{The opposite} — \emph{le soleil}, \emph{la lune}.) Can you work a German noun's gender out from the thing? (\textbf{No}.) Next: the day named for it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Sonntag]{Sonntag — \textquotedblleft{}Sunday\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C07-sonntag}



\begin{quote}
The pattern again, on the noun from a moment ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Sonntag}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Sonntag} — \textquotedblleft{}Sunday.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Sonne} plus \emph{Tag}, with the \emph{e} dropped in the compound. English says the same two words: \emph{sun} and \emph{day}.

\begin{culture}
\emph{Mittwoch} showed the Church taking a god out of the week. This day shows where it did \textbf{not}.

Romance renamed Sunday completely, for the \textbf{Lord}: Spanish \emph{domingo}, French \emph{dimanche}, both from Latin \emph{dies dominicus}. The sun was pushed out entirely. German and English kept the sun.

So the same institution rewrote one German day and left another alone, and the week records both decisions side by side. \emph{Mittwoch} is where it intervened; \emph{Sonntag} is where it did not.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Sonntag\textquotedblright{}
  \item its pieces — \textquotedblleft{}Sonne, Tag\textquotedblright{}
  \item what Romance did instead — \textquotedblleft{}domingo, dimanche\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two decisions — \textquotedblleft{}Mittwoch rewritten, Sonntag left alone\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Sonntag — Sunday.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}Sunday.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Sonntag}.) What are its two pieces? (\emph{\textbf{Sonne}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{Tag}}.) What did Spanish name the day for instead? (\textbf{The Lord} — \emph{domingo}.) Which German day did the Church rewrite? (\emph{\textbf{Mittwoch}}.) Next: a word that is not German at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Sabbat]{der Sabbat — \textquotedblleft{}the Sabbath\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C07-sabbat}



\begin{quote}
Every word in this week so far has been Germanic. Here is the one that is not — and it did not come from Latin either.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Sabbat}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Sabbat} — \textquotedblleft{}the Sabbath,\textquotedblright{} the day of rest.
\end{quote}

Hebrew \emph{shabbāt} means \textquotedblleft{}to rest.\textquotedblright{} Greek-speaking Christians took it as \emph{sábbaton} and carried it north, and German has it as \emph{Sabbat}.

Hold the word on its own for a moment before the next lesson does anything with it. Its road is the point: \textbf{Hebrew to Greek to German}, with no Germanic ancestor and no Latin one either. It is the only word in the German week that came from outside Europe.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Sabbat\textquotedblright{}
  \item the road — \textquotedblleft{}shabbāt, sábbaton, Sabbat\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it means — \textquotedblleft{}rest\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Sabbat — the Sabbath.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the Sabbath.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Sabbat}.) What does the Hebrew root mean? (\textbf{To rest}.) Which language carried it north? (\textbf{Greek}.) Is it Germanic or Latin? (\textbf{Neither}.) Next: the day it became.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Samstag]{Samstag — the day that is not Saturn's}

\label{lesson:GE-C07-samstag}



\begin{quote}
The second break in the pattern, and a bigger one than \emph{Mittwoch}. That day lost its god. This one was never Germanic at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Samstag}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Samstag} — \textquotedblleft{}Saturday.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

It ends in \emph{Tag}, so the shape looks intact. What sits in front of it is not a god: it is \emph{Sabbat}, worn down. \textbf{Sam(s)- + Tag} — \textquotedblleft{}the Sabbath day.\textquotedblright{}

English kept the Roman planet here. \emph{Saturday} is \textbf{Saturn's day}, the one Roman name the Germanic swap never replaced. German did replace it, but not with a god of its own.

\begin{cousinweb}
The road this word travelled is longer than any other in the chapter:

Hebrew \emph{shabbāt}, \textquotedblleft{}to rest,\textquotedblright{} became Greek \emph{sábbaton}, and Greek-speaking Christians carried it north into German as \emph{Sabbat}. From there it wore down to the \emph{Sams-} you say now.

So \textbf{German \emph{Samstag} and Spanish \emph{sábado} are the same word} — both are the Sabbath. And English, which usually stands beside German in this chapter, is the odd one out: it alone still points at a Roman planet.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
This is the distinction you were given with the months, arriving again on a different word.

The weekday names are the first kind of word: everyday, inherited, hard to displace — which is why six of them are still Germanic after fifteen hundred years. \emph{Samstag} is the second kind. It came with an institution, and it came in whole, exactly as the month names did.

So one week contains both answers to the same question. Six days a language kept, and one it bought.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Samstag\textquotedblright{}
  \item the road — \textquotedblleft{}shabbāt, sábbaton, Sabbat, Samstag\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}Samstag, sábado: the same Sabbath\textquotedblright{}
  \item the odd one — \textquotedblleft{}Saturday still points at Saturn\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Samstag — the Sabbath, not Saturn.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}Saturday.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Samstag}.) Is it Saturn's day? (\textbf{No} — the Sabbath's.) Which language did it reach German through? (\textbf{Greek}, from Hebrew.) Which Spanish day is the same word? (\emph{\textbf{Sábado}}.) Which kind of word is it — kept or bought? (\textbf{Bought}, like the month names.) Next: the day the Church left alone.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Sonnabend]{Sonnabend — Saturday, in the north}

\label{lesson:GE-C07-sonnabend}



\begin{quote}
One more Saturday. This one you can read before you are told what it means, because both halves are already yours.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Sonnabend}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Sonnabend} — \textquotedblleft{}Saturday,\textquotedblright{} in northern Germany.
\end{quote}

\emph{Sonn-} is the sun and \emph{-abend} is the evening, both of which you own. It is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Sun-eve}\textquotedblright{}: the evening before Sunday, standing in for the whole day.

That is the same reckoning English keeps in \emph{Christmas Eve} and \emph{New Year's Eve} — the day taking its name from the night that runs up to it.

\begin{culture}
Both words are correct German and a speaker will use one or the other by where they are from: \textbf{Sonnabend} in the north, \textbf{Samstag} in the south and west, with \emph{Samstag} the more widely used of the two.

So Saturday has two names in German and neither is a mistake — which is worth knowing before you hear the one you did not learn and assume you misheard it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Sonnabend\textquotedblright{}
  \item its two halves — \textquotedblleft{}Sonne, Abend\textquotedblright{}
  \item both Saturdays — \textquotedblleft{}Samstag, Sonnabend\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Sonnabend — Sun-eve.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the northern word for Saturday. (\textbf{Sonnabend}.) What are its two halves? (\emph{\textbf{Sonne}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{Abend}}.) What does it literally mean? (\textbf{Sun-eve}.) Which word is used more widely? (\emph{\textbf{Samstag}}.) Next: the whole week, said through.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — all seven}

\label{lesson:GE-C07-wochentage-2}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Seven days, five gods, and two places where something else got in.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the whole week}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{what is in it} \\
\midrule
\emph{Montag} & the moon \\
\emph{Dienstag} & Tiw \\
\emph{Mittwoch} & mid-week — the Church took the god out \\
\emph{Donnerstag} & Donar \\
\emph{Freitag} & Frija \\
\emph{Samstag} & the Sabbath — bought, not inherited \\
\emph{Sonntag} & the sun \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Five gods, one edit, one import. Run them in order until the list is one motion rather than seven remembered words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all seven in order, from \emph{Montag} to \emph{Sonntag}
  \item the two Saturdays — \textquotedblleft{}Samstag, Sonnabend\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two breaks — \textquotedblleft{}Mittwoch: no god. Samstag: not Germanic.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the shape that holds for the other five — \textquotedblleft{}a god, then Tag\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch, Donnerstag, Freitag, Samstag, Sonntag.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run all seven without prompting. Which day has no god? (\emph{\textbf{Mittwoch}}.) Which is not a Germanic word at all? (\emph{\textbf{Samstag}} — the Sabbath.) Which day did the Church rename in Romance but leave alone here? (\emph{\textbf{Sonntag}}.) Which day has two names? (\textbf{Saturday} — \emph{Samstag} and \emph{Sonnabend}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
